overview: The UPDATE statement is the DML command used to modify the values of existing rows in a table.
It uses SET to assign new values to one or more columns and a WHERE clause to restrict which rows are changed.
UPDATE can derive new values from subqueries or other tables (UPDATE ... FROM / UPDATE with JOIN), and many dialects support a RETURNING clause to see the modified rows.
learningObjectives: Write correct UPDATE statements that set single and multiple columns scoped by a WHERE clause.
Understand the critical danger that an UPDATE without WHERE modifies every row in the table.
Apply correlated subqueries, UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN, transactional safety, and RETURNING to update data reliably.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: UPDATE is a DML statement of the form UPDATE table SET column = expression [, ...] [FROM source] [WHERE predicate]. It evaluates the predicate to select target rows and assigns the SET expressions to them. All modifications occur within a transaction and must satisfy table constraints; without a WHERE clause every row in the table is updated.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: UPDATE changes data that is already in a table. You say which table, which columns to change with SET, the new values, and which rows to change with WHERE. The most important rule: if you forget the WHERE clause, you change every single row in the table.
coreConcept.historicalContext: UPDATE has been a core SQL statement since the original SQL specification and SQL-86. The ability to update from joined data (UPDATE ... FROM in SQL Server/PostgreSQL, multi-table UPDATE in MySQL) and the RETURNING clause (PostgreSQL, Oracle) were later additions that made data-correction and ETL workflows more expressive. The accidental full-table update remains one of the most infamous operational incidents in database history.

whyItMatters.business: UPDATE keeps records current: order statuses, account balances, inventory levels, and customer details all change over time and must be modified accurately.
whyItMatters.engineering: Correctly scoped, set-based UPDATEs are the efficient way to correct or transform existing data; a missing WHERE or bad join can corrupt an entire table in one statement.
whyItMatters.scalability: Set-based UPDATEs that touch only the necessary rows, backed by good indexes on the WHERE predicate, avoid full-table scans and excessive locking under load.
whyItMatters.cost: A mis-scoped UPDATE can require costly restores and data reconciliation; disciplined, transactional updates avoid that operational expense.
whyItMatters.reliability: Wrapping UPDATEs in transactions with verified WHERE clauses (and previewing with SELECT) prevents catastrophic data loss and enables rollback if results are wrong.

coreComponents.name: Target Table
coreComponents.definition: The table whose existing rows will be modified.
coreComponents.purpose: To identify where the changes are applied.
coreComponents.responsibilities: All resulting row values must still satisfy the table's constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FK, CHECK).

coreComponents.name: SET Clause
coreComponents.definition: One or more column = expression assignments specifying the new values.
coreComponents.purpose: To define what changes; expressions may reference the existing column value or other columns.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Each assignment is computed from the row's pre-update values, allowing self-referential updates like balance = balance - 50.

coreComponents.name: WHERE Clause (Row Scope)
coreComponents.definition: A predicate that selects which rows are updated.
coreComponents.purpose: To restrict the update to the intended rows; its absence updates ALL rows.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Must be specific enough to target only the desired rows; should be index-supported for performance.

internalWorking: The engine evaluates the WHERE predicate (and any FROM/join) to identify the set of qualifying rows.
For each qualifying row, the SET expressions are evaluated using that row's current values, and the new values are validated against constraints.

Affected rows are locked and rewritten; indexes on changed columns are updated. In MVCC engines (e.g., PostgreSQL) an UPDATE writes a new row version and marks the old one dead rather than editing in place.
All changes happen inside the current transaction; on COMMIT they become durable and visible, while ROLLBACK discards them entirely.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Evaluate WHERE/JOIN -> Select target rows -> Lock rows -> Compute SET expressions -> Validate constraints -> Write new values & update indexes -> Commit or Rollback
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Application issues UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE account_id = 7.
2. The engine locates account 7 via an index on account_id and acquires a lock on that row.
3. It computes balance - 50 from the current balance and checks the result against a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint.
4. The new balance is written; with RETURNING balance the new value is sent back to the application.
5. On COMMIT the change is durable; the row count affected (1) is reported.

keyTerminology.meaning: The condition that determines which rows an UPDATE affects.
keyTerminology.importance: Its presence and correctness are the single most important safeguard against mass, unintended data modification.

keyTerminology.meaning: Syntax that lets an UPDATE derive new values by joining the target to other tables.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables efficient, set-based correction and enrichment of data from related tables in one statement.

keyTerminology.meaning: A subquery in the SET or WHERE clause that references the outer row being updated.
keyTerminology.importance: Lets each row compute its new value from related data, but must return at most one value per row.

importantConcepts.explanation: UPDATE without a WHERE clause modifies every row in the table. This is valid SQL and executes silently, so it is a leading cause of catastrophic data incidents. Always verify scope with a SELECT first and run inside a transaction.

Running UPDATE inside BEGIN ... COMMIT lets you inspect the affected row count (and RETURNING output) before committing, and ROLLBACK if the result is wrong. RETURNING (PostgreSQL/Oracle) or OUTPUT (SQL Server) shows exactly which rows changed.

variationsAndTypes: **Single-column UPDATE:** SET one column for matching rows.
**Multi-column UPDATE:** SET several columns in one statement, e.g., SET status = 'x', updated_at = now().
**UPDATE with subquery:** Derive new values or filter rows using a correlated or scalar subquery.
**UPDATE ... FROM / multi-table UPDATE:** Update the target using values joined from other tables (PostgreSQL/SQL Server FROM; MySQL multi-table syntax).
**UPDATE ... RETURNING / OUTPUT:** Return the modified rows for confirmation or downstream use.
advantages: **In-place modification:** Changes existing rows without delete-and-reinsert, preserving identity and references.
**Set-based and efficient:** One statement can correct or transform millions of rows without application loops.
**Expressive:** Subqueries and joins let new values be derived from related data.
**Transaction-safe:** Updates can be previewed, verified via row counts/RETURNING, and rolled back.
disadvantages: **Catastrophic if mis-scoped:** A missing or wrong WHERE clause silently updates every targeted row.
**Locking and contention:** Large updates hold locks and can block concurrent transactions or cause deadlocks.
**Write amplification:** MVCC engines create new row versions, inflating table bloat and triggering vacuum/compaction.
**Index and log overhead:** Updating indexed columns and writing large transaction logs is costly at scale.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use UPDATE to modify existing rows in place when identity and foreign-key references must be preserved, scoping with an indexed WHERE clause and wrapping risky changes in transactions.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid huge single UPDATEs that lock a table for a long time; batch them in chunks. Avoid UPDATE for high-churn columns where an append-only/event-sourced design or partitioning would scale better.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: UPDATE is like editing entries in a ledger with a pencil. SET is the new figure you write, and WHERE is pointing to the specific line you mean. If you skip pointing to a line (no WHERE), you erase and rewrite every line in the ledger. Editing inside a transaction is like using an undo-able draft you can discard before it becomes permanent.

commonMisconceptions.myth: UPDATE only changes the rows I intend, the WHERE is optional detail.
commonMisconceptions.reality: WHERE is the only thing limiting scope. Without it, UPDATE changes every row in the table, and the database executes it without warning.

commonMisconceptions.myth: SET balance = balance - 50 reads the column after it is updated.
commonMisconceptions.reality: All SET expressions are evaluated from each row's pre-update values, so multiple assignments in the same statement see the original values, not each other's new values.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Scope updates with indexed predicates and batch very large updates into chunks (e.g., by primary-key ranges) to limit lock duration and log growth. Update only the rows that actually need changing.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Run risky updates inside an explicit transaction, preview with SELECT, verify the affected row count, and ROLLBACK if it is wrong before COMMIT. Keep recent backups for recovery.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Transactions guarantee all-or-nothing semantics, so a crash mid-update leaves a consistent state recoverable from the log. Idempotent updates make safe retries possible.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Monitor rows-affected counts, update latency, lock waits, deadlocks, and (in MVCC systems) table bloat and vacuum activity caused by heavy updates.
productionConsiderations.security: Use parameterized statements to prevent SQL injection in SET/WHERE values, and restrict UPDATE privileges and column-level permissions to least privilege.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Touch fewer rows and fewer indexed columns to cut I/O, log, and vacuum cost. Avoid no-op updates that set columns to their current values.
productionConsiderations.performance: Index the WHERE predicate and join columns; avoid updating indexed/PK columns unnecessarily. Batch large updates to control transaction-log and lock pressure.

codeExamples.title: Single-column, Multi-column, and the Danger of a Missing WHERE
codeExamples.overview: Shows scoped single- and multi-column updates and contrasts them with the catastrophic full-table update caused by omitting WHERE.
codeExamples.code:
-- Update a single column for ONE row (scoped by primary key)
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'shipped'
WHERE order_id = 101;

-- Update multiple columns at once for matching rows
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'shipped',
    shipped_at = now()
WHERE status = 'paid' AND order_date < '2026-06-01';

-- DANGER: no WHERE clause updates EVERY row in the table!
-- UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped';   -- sets ALL orders to shipped

-- Safe pattern: preview the scope first
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE order_id = 101;  -- confirm 1 row
codeExamples.breakdown: The first statement changes one column for a single keyed row. The second sets two columns for all rows matching a compound predicate. The commented statement shows that omitting WHERE updates every row; the final SELECT illustrates previewing the affected scope before running the UPDATE.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Statement 1 reports 1 row affected. Statement 2 reports N rows affected (the matching paid orders). The no-WHERE statement would report all rows in orders affected.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting WHERE; an overly broad predicate; violating a CHECK or NOT NULL constraint with the new value. Multi-column SET expressions all read pre-update values.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Ensure the WHERE columns are indexed. Always run the equivalent SELECT count(*) first, and execute risky updates inside a transaction.

codeExamples.title: UPDATE with Subquery, UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN
codeExamples.overview: Derives new values from related tables using a correlated subquery and the more efficient set-based UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN forms.
codeExamples.code:
-- Correlated subquery: set each customer's last_order_date
UPDATE customers c
SET last_order_date = (
    SELECT MAX(o.order_date)
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);

-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server: UPDATE ... FROM (set-based, usually faster)
UPDATE customers AS c
SET total_spent = agg.total
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
) AS agg
WHERE c.customer_id = agg.customer_id;

-- MySQL multi-table UPDATE with JOIN (equivalent)
UPDATE customers c
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) agg
  ON c.customer_id = agg.customer_id
SET c.total_spent = agg.total;
codeExamples.breakdown: The correlated subquery computes a per-customer aggregate but re-runs per row. The UPDATE ... FROM (PostgreSQL/SQL Server) and the JOIN form (MySQL) join the target to a pre-aggregated derived table, applying values in one set-based pass that is typically far faster.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Each customer's last_order_date and total_spent are set from their orders. Customers with no orders are skipped by the EXISTS / join.
codeExamples.commonIssues: A correlated subquery returning more than one row errors; a join that matches multiple source rows produces unpredictable assignments. MySQL and PostgreSQL/SQL Server use different join syntax.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN over correlated subqueries for large tables. Pre-aggregate in a derived table and ensure join keys are indexed.

codeExamples.title: Transactional Safety with RETURNING
codeExamples.overview: Wraps a balance transfer in a transaction, previews and verifies the change with RETURNING, and rolls back on error.
codeExamples.breakdown: Both updates run in one transaction so they commit or roll back together. The debit's WHERE includes balance >= 100, so insufficient funds yield 0 rows affected; RETURNING surfaces the new balances. ROLLBACK discards both updates if anything is wrong.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: If account 1 has at least 100, both updates report 1 row affected and return the new balances; COMMIT makes the transfer durable. If not, the debit affects 0 rows and the operator issues ROLLBACK.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting to check the affected row count before COMMIT; running the two updates outside a transaction (leaving money debited but not credited on failure).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use RETURNING/OUTPUT to confirm results without a separate SELECT. Keep transactions short to minimize lock duration and contention.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A subscription business must apply a monthly billing run: mark active subscriptions as billed, advance their next_bill_date, and flag those whose payment failed, all without accidentally touching cancelled or trial accounts.
endToEndExample.inputData: A subscriptions table (subscription_id, customer_id, status, next_bill_date, amount) and a payments table (subscription_id, period, success) produced by the payment gateway.
endToEndExample.architecture: PostgreSQL OLTP database. A billing job runs scoped UPDATE statements inside a transaction, joining subscriptions to the latest payment results and using RETURNING to log outcomes.
processingSteps: 1. BEGIN a transaction for the billing run.
2. UPDATE subscriptions SET status = 'past_due' FROM payments p WHERE subscriptions.subscription_id = p.subscription_id AND p.success = false AND subscriptions.status = 'active'.
3. UPDATE subscriptions SET status = 'billed', next_bill_date = next_bill_date + INTERVAL '1 month' WHERE status = 'active' AND next_bill_date <= CURRENT_DATE RETURNING subscription_id.
4. Verify the affected row counts match expectations from a pre-run SELECT count(*).
5. COMMIT if counts are correct, otherwise ROLLBACK the whole run.
endToEndExample.output: Active, due subscriptions are advanced and marked billed; subscriptions with failed payments are flagged past_due; cancelled and trial subscriptions are untouched because the WHERE clauses scope status = 'active'.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Compare rows-affected to the expected count of due subscriptions; alert if it deviates (a sign of a WHERE bug). Track update latency, lock waits, and the RETURNING-logged subscription IDs for audit.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: The whole run is one transaction: if any step errors or counts look wrong, ROLLBACK leaves all subscriptions unchanged so the run can be safely re-attempted after fixing the issue.
endToEndExample.finalResult: An auditable, transactional billing run where carefully scoped UPDATE ... FROM statements modify only the intended subscriptions, with RETURNING providing a record of exactly what changed and the ability to roll back as a safety net.

industryUseCases.problem: Adjusting account balances during transfers and payments where partial application would be catastrophic.
industryUseCases.solution: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance +/- amount with a guard predicate (balance >= amount) inside a transaction, using RETURNING to confirm the new balance.
industryUseCases.benefits: Atomic, all-or-nothing money movement; guard clauses prevent overdrafts; rollback on any failure.

industryUseCases.problem: Transitioning order and shipment statuses as they move through fulfillment.
industryUseCases.solution: Scoped multi-column UPDATEs (SET status, timestamp) filtered by current status and time, often joined to fulfillment data via UPDATE ... FROM.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate state machines, only valid transitions applied, efficient set-based status changes.

industryUseCases.problem: Enriching and correcting dimension tables with values computed from fact tables.
industryUseCases.solution: UPDATE ... FROM / MERGE joining the dimension to pre-aggregated fact data to set derived columns like total_spent or last_seen.
industryUseCases.benefits: Set-based correction without row-by-row loops; fast bulk enrichment; consistent derived attributes.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Large UPDATEs should be chunked (e.g., loop over primary-key ranges, updating N rows per transaction) to bound lock duration and transaction-log growth. Always restrict with an indexed WHERE predicate and update only rows that truly need changing to avoid no-op write amplification.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Transactions provide all-or-nothing guarantees, so a crash mid-update is rolled back during recovery from the WAL/redo log. Designing updates to be idempotent (e.g., status transitions guarded by current status) makes re-runs after failure safe.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Committed updates replicate to standbys; synchronous replication ensures the change survives failover at the cost of latency, while asynchronous replication is faster but risks losing the most recent commits on a sudden failover.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because UPDATE overwrites prior values, recovering from a bad update relies on backups and point-in-time recovery via the transaction log. This is exactly why a missing-WHERE incident is so damaging and why soft-delete/versioning patterns are sometimes preferred.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Index WHERE and join columns; avoid updating indexed or primary-key columns when possible; batch large updates; in MVCC engines schedule vacuum/compaction after heavy updates to reclaim space from dead row versions.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Minimize rows and columns touched, skip no-op updates (WHERE col <> newval), and batch to reduce log and replication volume, directly lowering compute and storage churn costs.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Parameterize all SET and WHERE values to prevent SQL injection. Grant UPDATE only on required tables/columns (column-level privileges) and consider triggers or row-level security to enforce who may modify which rows.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track rows-affected per statement against expectations, update latency percentiles, lock waits, deadlock counts, and bloat/vacuum metrics. An unexpected rows-affected spike is an early signal of a WHERE-clause defect.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Constraints (CHECK, NOT NULL, FK) validate post-update values; guarded predicates (e.g., balance >= amount, status = 'active') enforce valid state transitions. Pre-run SELECT counts validate scope.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Use RETURNING/OUTPUT to log exactly which rows changed for audit trails. Alert on updates affecting more rows than a threshold, which often indicates an accidental full-table update.

recommendedPractices: **Never run UPDATE without verifying the WHERE clause:** Preview scope with SELECT count(*) using the same predicate first.
**Wrap risky updates in a transaction:** BEGIN, run, verify row counts/RETURNING, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
**Prefer set-based UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN:** Derive values from related tables in one pass instead of correlated-subquery loops.
**Index the WHERE and join columns:** Avoid full-table scans and reduce lock footprint.
engineeringStandards: All UPDATE values come from parameterized queries; no user input is string-concatenated into SET/WHERE.
Bulk corrective updates are reviewed, run in a transaction, and chunked above a defined row threshold.
State-transition updates include a guard on the current state (e.g., WHERE status = 'active') for idempotency.
designRecommendations: Index columns frequently used in UPDATE predicates and joins.
Guard money/inventory updates with predicates (balance >= amount) rather than relying on application checks alone.
For high-churn audit-critical data, consider append-only/versioned designs instead of in-place UPDATE.
namingConventions: Use clear aliases in UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN (e.g., target c, source agg) to avoid ambiguous column references.
Name derived/aggregate subqueries meaningfully (e.g., agg, latest) so SET expressions read clearly.
documentationStandards: Document the intended scope and guard conditions of any recurring corrective/batch UPDATE.
Record which dialect-specific syntax (UPDATE ... FROM vs. multi-table JOIN) the codebase uses.
Note constraints that the new values must satisfy and the expected affected row count.
testingStrategies: Test that the WHERE clause limits changes to exactly the intended rows (assert affected count).
Test idempotency by running a guarded state-transition update twice and asserting no extra changes.
Test rollback by simulating a mid-transaction failure and asserting the table is unchanged.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running UPDATE without a WHERE clause.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Writing the statement top-down and executing before adding the predicate, or copy-pasting and forgetting the filter.
commonMistakes.impact: Every row in the table is modified, often irreversibly, requiring a restore from backup to recover.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always include and verify WHERE; preview with SELECT count(*) on the same predicate and run inside a transaction so you can ROLLBACK.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a correlated subquery in SET that can return multiple rows.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The join relationship is not actually one-to-one, so the subquery yields more than one value per outer row.
commonMistakes.impact: The statement errors (subquery returned more than one row) or, in lenient engines, assigns an unpredictable value.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Aggregate the subquery (MAX, SUM) or use UPDATE ... FROM with a pre-aggregated, deduplicated source and indexed join keys.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running a huge UPDATE as a single transaction.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is simplest to issue one statement covering millions of rows.
commonMistakes.impact: Long-held locks block other transactions, the transaction log balloons, and replication lags or the statement times out.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Batch the update into chunks (by key range) with periodic commits, keeping each transaction short.

comparisonSection.explanation: A correlated subquery re-evaluates per target row and must return a single value, which is simple but can be slow and error-prone on many rows. UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN joins to a pre-aggregated source and applies values in one set-based pass, which is typically much faster and clearer for large tables.

comparisonSection.feature: Modifying existing data vs. removing it
comparisonSection.explanation: UPDATE preserves row identity and foreign-key references while changing values, ideal for status changes and balance adjustments. DELETE + INSERT recreates rows, which can break references and generate new identities, and is rarely preferable to a direct UPDATE for editing existing records.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does UPDATE do and what is the role of the WHERE clause?
beginnerQuestions.answer: UPDATE modifies the values of existing rows. The SET clause assigns new values and the WHERE clause selects which rows are changed. Without WHERE, UPDATE changes every row in the table.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress that WHERE is the scope control and that omitting it is dangerous, not optional cosmetics.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you update multiple columns in a single statement?
beginnerQuestions.answer: List comma-separated assignments in the SET clause, e.g., UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped', shipped_at = now() WHERE order_id = 101. All expressions are evaluated from the row's pre-update values.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Mention that the assignments read original values, so SET a = b, b = a swaps using the old values.

intermediateQuestions.question: What happens if you run an UPDATE without a WHERE clause, and how do you guard against it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: It updates every row in the table, which is valid SQL and executes without warning. Guards include previewing with SELECT count(*) on the intended predicate, running inside a transaction so you can ROLLBACK, enabling safe-update mode (MySQL --safe-updates), and reviewing the affected row count before COMMIT.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is a classic interview probe on operational discipline; cite the transaction + preview pattern.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you update a table using values from another table?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use UPDATE ... FROM (PostgreSQL/SQL Server) or a multi-table UPDATE ... JOIN (MySQL) to join the target to a source/derived table, or a correlated subquery in SET. The set-based join form is preferred for large tables.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show both the subquery and join approaches and note the dialect syntax differences.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you safely apply a corrective UPDATE to millions of rows in production?
advancedQuestions.answer: Batch it: loop over primary-key ranges updating a bounded number of rows per transaction with periodic commits, scope each batch with an indexed WHERE, and make the update idempotent (guard on current state). Verify counts, run during low traffic, and keep transactions short to avoid long locks, log bloat, and replication lag.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate awareness of locking, log/WAL growth, replication, and idempotent batching.

advancedQuestions.question: In an MVCC database like PostgreSQL, what is the cost of a large UPDATE and how do you mitigate it?
advancedQuestions.answer: Each updated row creates a new version and marks the old one dead, causing table/index bloat and extra I/O; HOT updates help only when no indexed column changes. Mitigate by updating fewer rows/columns, avoiding indexed-column updates, batching, and running VACUUM (or autovacuum) afterward to reclaim space.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Shows deeper engine knowledge of write amplification and vacuum/bloat.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You need to give a 10% discount to all orders from a specific customer placed last month, but you are worried about accidentally updating other customers' orders.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Identify the exact predicate (customer_id and date range). Preview the affected rows with SELECT, then run the UPDATE inside a transaction, verify the affected count matches the preview, and only then COMMIT.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: First SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date >= '2026-05-01' AND order_date < '2026-06-01'. Then BEGIN; UPDATE orders SET amount = amount * 0.9 WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date >= '2026-05-01' AND order_date < '2026-06-01'; confirm the row count equals the preview; COMMIT (or ROLLBACK if it differs).

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a status-transition system for orders moving through pending -> paid -> shipped -> delivered, updated by multiple concurrent workers.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Model each transition as a guarded UPDATE: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped', shipped_at = now() WHERE order_id = :id AND status = 'paid'. The current-status guard makes the transition idempotent and prevents invalid jumps; the affected row count tells the worker whether it won the transition.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Guarded updates avoid explicit locks and are naturally idempotent, but hot rows can contend; optimistic concurrency (a version column in the WHERE) reduces blocking at the cost of retry logic.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Index order_id and status, keep transactions short, partition orders by date, and let workers retry on a zero-affected-rows result. Use RETURNING to confirm and log the transition for audit.

How can you preview which rows an UPDATE will affect before running it?
What does MySQL's safe-updates mode do?
How are SET expressions evaluated relative to the row's current values?
How would you recover from an accidental full-table UPDATE?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: UPDATE modifies existing rows: SET assigns new column values and WHERE scopes which rows change; without WHERE it changes every row.
keyConcepts: SET: assign one or more columns from expressions on pre-update values.
WHERE: the only scope control; omitting it updates ALL rows.
UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN: derive values from related tables (set-based).
Correlated subquery: per-row derived value, must return one value.
Transaction + RETURNING: preview, verify, and roll back risky updates.
Batching: chunk huge updates to limit locks and log growth.
commands: UPDATE t SET col = val WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE t SET a = 'x', b = now() WHERE cond;
UPDATE t SET c = (SELECT MAX(x) FROM s WHERE s.tid = t.id) WHERE EXISTS (...);
UPDATE t SET c = agg.v FROM (SELECT id, ... AS v FROM s GROUP BY id) agg WHERE t.id = agg.id;  -- PostgreSQL/SQL Server
UPDATE t JOIN s ON t.id = s.id SET t.c = s.v;  -- MySQL
BEGIN; UPDATE t SET ... WHERE ... RETURNING *; COMMIT;  -- or ROLLBACK
interviewPoints: No WHERE = full-table update; always verify scope.
SET reads pre-update values for all assignments.
Prefer UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN over correlated subqueries at scale.
Wrap risky updates in a transaction and verify row counts.
Batch large updates to avoid long locks and log bloat.
quickNotes: Always preview with SELECT count(*) using the same WHERE before an UPDATE.
RETURNING (PostgreSQL/Oracle) and OUTPUT (SQL Server) show the modified rows.
MySQL safe-updates mode blocks UPDATE/DELETE without a key-based WHERE.
In MVCC engines an UPDATE writes a new row version; VACUUM reclaims the old ones.
Guard state transitions with the current state in WHERE to make updates idempotent.
Parameterize SET/WHERE values to prevent SQL injection.

keyTakeaways: UPDATE modifies existing rows using SET for new values and WHERE to scope which rows change.
An UPDATE without a WHERE clause modifies every row in the table and runs silently, so verifying scope is the single most important safeguard.
Derive new values from related data with UPDATE ... FROM / JOIN (preferred for large tables) or correlated subqueries that return a single value.
Wrap risky updates in a transaction, preview with SELECT, verify the affected row count, and use RETURNING/OUTPUT before committing, rolling back if results are wrong.
Batch very large updates, index the WHERE/join columns, and guard state transitions for idempotency to control locking, log growth, and contention.
